title: Who is Stephen Miller? From a Santa Monica call-in show to the office next to the president’s, in six acts
dek: He is 41, has worked for Trump longer than anyone in the building, and has written the administration’s immigration policy twice. The record he made himself, from the Larry Elder Show at 16 to the 3,000-a-day order, and what is on his desk Monday.
body:
Stephen Miller is 41, has worked for Donald Trump longer than anyone else in the building, and has now written the administration’s immigration policy twice [8][13]. On Monday he becomes White House chief of staff [13]. Most of what is known about him is on the record, because he put it there: on talk radio at 16, in a student newspaper column at 20, in 900 emails to Breitbart editors at 30, and in a decade of television since. Here is that record, in six acts.

## Act one: Santa Monica, 1985 to 2003

Stephen Miller was born on August 23, 1985, in Santa Monica, California, the second of three children of Michael Miller, a lawyer who worked in the family real estate business, and Miriam Miller, a social worker [1]. He entered Santa Monica High School in 1999, in one of the most liberal cities in the country, and found his voice as the school’s conservative contrarian [1][2][10].

The voice was literal. He began calling in to Larry Elder’s talk-radio show to complain about the school, and by his own count appeared on it 69 times; he brought Elder to campus [1][2]. He pushed the school to recite the Pledge of Allegiance every day, and reported the result as a “huge victory” [1]. In 2002 he ran for student announcer and lost after a speech questioning why students should pick up their own trash when janitors were paid to [1]. David Horowitz, the conservative activist who would become his mentor, first met him in those years [2]. He graduated in 2003 [1].

## Act two: Duke, 2003 to 2007

At Duke he studied political science, founded the campus chapter of Horowitz’s Students for Academic Freedom in 2004, and invited Horowitz to speak, which drew protests from students and faculty [1][2]. From September 2005 he wrote a column for The Chronicle called “Miller Time,” every other Monday: 25 bylines over 19 months, opening with “Welcome to Leftist University” and closing with “Farewell” on April 23, 2007 [4][5]. The topics were liberal bias in hiring, the pay gap, Christmas, affirmative action and what he called “divisive multiculturalism” [5].

By his junior year he had joined the Duke Conservative Union, and he was its executive director as a senior [1]. Through it he met Richard Spencer, and the two organized an immigration debate in March 2007; Miller has since told The Washington Post that he condemns Spencer and had no relationship with him [1]. The event that made him nationally known was the 2006 lacrosse case, in which he defended three players accused of rape, in print and on Fox News and Nancy Grace’s show, a year before the state attorney general declared them innocent [3][8]. That story is told in a companion piece. John Burness, then a Duke senior vice president, remembered him this way: “He always believed he was on the side of morality” [3].

## Act three: Capitol Hill, 2007 to 2016

He moved to Washington in 2007, at 22, and was press secretary to Rep. Michele Bachmann of Minnesota by that December, and later to Rep. John Shadegg of Arizona, on Horowitz’s recommendation [1][2]. In June 2009 Horowitz recommended him again, to Sen. Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who made him press secretary and then communications director [1][2]. He spent seven years with Sessions [3].

The defining fight of those years was the 2013 immigration bill, the Border Security, Economic Opportunity and Immigration Modernization Act, which passed the Senate and was never taken up by the House; Miller supplied House staffers with a binder of talking points against it [1]. That year he, Sessions and Steve Bannon met at Bannon’s Washington home after the party’s 2012 losses and agreed that immigration and trade were the issues that could win working-class voters [2]. “And that guy a couple years later turned out to be Donald Trump,” Bannon told Frontline [2].

The other record of those years came out in November 2019, when the Southern Poverty Law Center published more than 900 emails Miller had sent to Breitbart editors between March 2015 and June 2016, provided by Katie McHugh, a former Breitbart editor [6]. In them he shared articles from the white nationalist site VDARE, recommended that Breitbart write about the novel “The Camp of the Saints,” repeatedly invoked Calvin Coolidge and the Immigration Act of 1924, and, after retailers pulled Confederate merchandise following the Charleston church massacre, suggested a story on “commie flags” [6][1]. Kurt Bardella, a former Breitbart spokesman, described him as “almost a de facto assignment editor” [1]. Democrats including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called for his resignation; the SPLC placed him on its list of extremists [7][1]. Miller is Jewish, and some of his defenders called the attacks antisemitic [7].

## Act four: the first term, 2016 to 2021

He joined the Trump campaign as a senior policy adviser in January 2016, was warming up rally crowds by March, and wrote the acceptance speech at that summer’s convention [1][3]. “I think he helped Trump find his voice,” Bannon told The Associated Press in 2017 [8]. He wrote the inaugural address, the 2017 speech to a joint session of Congress and the 2018 State of the Union [1].

As senior adviser for policy he co-wrote the first executive orders with Bannon, including the January 2017 travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, a revised version of which the Supreme Court upheld [1][8]. He pressed Trump to end DACA, which Trump announced in September 2017 [1][8]. He pushed the refugee cap down from the 110,000 of the Obama years toward 15,000; it was set at 30,000 for fiscal 2019 [1]. In April 2018 he backed the zero-tolerance policy that prosecuted nearly every adult crossing the border without papers and separated their children from them, until Trump reversed it by executive order after the backlash [1][8]. In 2019 he led the public-charge rule, which favored wealthier applicants for green cards [1].

Bannon was out within a year of the inauguration, Sessions by late 2018; Miller stayed, which was the point of Frontline’s 2019 profile, “Last Man Standing” [2]. After the 2020 election he argued on Fox News that an “alternate slate of electors” could still deliver the presidency to Trump, wrote the speech Trump gave on January 6, and in April 2022 testified privately to the House committee investigating the attack [1][8].

## Act five: the wilderness, 2021 to 2024

In April 2021 he founded America First Legal, a group to challenge the Biden administration in court, with Mark Meadows and Matthew Whitaker on its board; any Biden policy the group “believes to be illegal” would be “fair game,” he told The Wall Street Journal [9]. The group also filed complaints accusing companies such as Nike of discriminating against white people [10].

He had married Katie Waldman, then a Trump administration communications aide, in February 2020 at the Trump hotel in Washington, with the president in attendance; they have four children [1][10]. She went on to be the spokeswoman for Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and is now a conservative podcaster [10]. Miller stayed close to Trump through the 2024 campaign, and on November 13, 2024, was named deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser [1][8].

## Act six: the second term, 2025 to now

He took both titles on January 20, 2025, and separated the Homeland Security Council from the National Security Council to run it himself [1]. The program he built is measured in a companion piece. Its headline was an order: in May 2025 he told Fox News the administration wanted “a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day,” and Axios reported that he and Kristi Noem had set it as a quota, which the Justice Department later denied in court [8][1]. He told ICE to arrest anyone in the country illegally, not only people with records, and named Home Depot parking lots as a place to find them [10]. In May 2025 he said the administration was considering suspending habeas corpus for immigrants; in April he said Kilmar Abrego Garcia had not been mistakenly deported, contradicting the Justice Department’s own filings [1]. He oversaw the federalization of the D.C. National Guard, and after Charlie Kirk’s assassination vowed to use the Justice and Homeland Security departments against what he called a “vast domestic terror movement” [1].

In 2026 his portfolio reached well past immigration. On the military strikes on suspected drug boats: “These are terrorists and they’re going to be killed” [10]. After the capture of Nicolás Maduro in January, he said the United States was “running Venezuela,” and he declined to rule out military action to take Greenland, saying nobody would fight the United States over it [10][1]. During the Iran war he threatened consequences “the likes of which has not been seen in modern history” [1]. When the Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship 6-3 on June 30, he called the ruling “destructive and outrageous” and wrote that “American citizenship is not the birthright of the world”; weeks later he announced a ban on “birth tourism” [11][10]. He joined the anti-fraud task force on benefit programs and helped lead October’s suspension of Microsoft and other companies from a green card labor program [13]. He is one of a handful of staffers who approve every executive order [10].

Two events this year define how his critics see him. On January 24, hours after Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a nurse filming them in Minneapolis, Miller called him a “domestic terrorist” and a “would-be assassin”; video reviewed by Reuters and others showed Pretti holding a phone, not a gun, and Miller later said the agents “may not have been following” protocol [10][8]. And on July 14, Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia graduate the administration held for 104 days, sued him along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Noem, her successor Markwayne Mullin and Todd Blanche under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, alleging a coordinated effort with the Heritage Foundation and two pro-Israel groups to target non-citizen Palestinian activists [12]. In “Regime Change,” the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan describe him as a domineering boss who regularly berated staff [10].

## Monday

Newsweek listed six things on his desk: the deportation program; a Democratic Congress that has promised to investigate him; the Iran war and the cartels; tariffs, which he has called the thing that “built America”; a possible Supreme Court vacancy that a Democratic Senate could block; and a MAGA coalition that lost Latino voters by 30 points on Tuesday, by CNN’s exit poll [14]. When the Senate confirmed Mullin to run Homeland Security in March, Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat who voted yes, said he looked forward to a secretary who did not take orders from Miller [15]. From Monday, the orders come from the office next to the president’s.
